claims.text: Adding 1–2 wt% CeO2 to the high-entropy alloy catalyst will stabilize active sites and enhance oxygen activation.
The starting catalyst is a nearly equiatomic, multi-element high-entropy alloy with low platinum-group-metal content.
CeO2 can be incorporated during synthesis or by post-synthesis treatment.
The catalyst is intended to operate under transient, low-temperature gasoline or hybrid exhaust conditions involving H2O, NO, thermal aging, and mileage-related degradation.
CeO2 addition creates a network that enhances oxygen-vacancy formation.
CeO2 stabilizes the catalyst's metal nanoparticles and reduces sintering.
The reversible Ce3+/Ce4+ redox capacity of CeO2 is associated with oxygen-vacancy formation.
CeO2-derived oxygen vacancies activate chemisorbed oxygen identified as Oβ.
Oxygen vacancies and enhanced oxygen mobility promote oxidation reactions.
The proposed CeO2 mechanism minimizes hydrothermal and thermal degradation of active sites.
Relative to the untreated catalyst, CeO2 doping will lower oxidation light-off temperatures.
Relative to the untreated catalyst, CeO2 doping will improve oxidation kinetics.
Relative to the untreated catalyst, CeO2 doping will enhance durability against hydrothermal and thermal aging.
The untreated high-entropy catalyst exhibits significant activity loss and durability problems under the stated operating conditions.
Performance improvement is specifically expected at a CeO2 loading of 1–2 wt%.
CeO2 loadings outside 1–2 wt% may provide diminished benefits or counteract catalytic activity.
The magnitudes of the light-off and long-term stability improvements, and the scalability of doping, remain uncertain.
A matched CeO2-doped versus untreated control experiment under simulated exhaust and aging conditions can test the hypothesis.
Failure to obtain statistically significant improvements in light-off, conversion, and structural stability relative to the untreated control would falsify the hypothesis.
